articles.title: IDEAS Collide: What would you do if vehicles stopped crashing?
articles.author: Lurah Lowery

paras.en: What if advanced driver assistance systems (ADAS) prevent collisions entirely, eliminating vehicle crashes? How would you bring business into your shop?

That was the food for thought from Justin Allen, Hunter Engineering regional trainer, one of seven speakers in this year’s Society of Collision Repair Specialists (SCRS) IDEAS Collide Showcase. The showcase was held Nov. 4 during this year’s SEMA Show in Las Vegas.
Allen encourages collision repair shops to be proactive and use their imagination so they’re prepared if business slows drastically.

“We’re in a major time of disruption,” Allen said. “I don’t think anybody would argue with that idea. ADAS stuff is changing the game. It’s changing the trade, changing the things we have to be prepared for.

“Currently, we’re dependent upon vehicles colliding with things, trees, houses, cars… When did that start happening? 135 years ago. So the collision business has been active for a long, long time. 1891 was the first time that occurred. And when did they start crashing even more? …the advent of that doggone cell phone. It’s not just for selfies; it’s for distractions while driving.”
Allen shared that by the early 2000s, more than 50% of households had cell phones, noting that now, everybody’s got one in their pocket.
Comparatively, only about a third of vehicles on the road use ADAS technology, he said.

“What does it mean for us that ADAS technology is getting better? We know fewer vehicles are actually being in collisions,” Allen said. “There’s more technology required… That’s creating more costs and repairs, and yet there’s more total vehicles. There’s an evolution occurring; change is taking place. We just get to decide what on Earth are we going to do about it?”
Allen suggests shops think of work to bring in-house rather than subletting.

“I want to encourage you to choose excitement,” he said. “You’ve got an opportunity to not be worried about what’s going to change in a negative direction. How can we capitalize on some good things going on here? Certainly, the automotive industry as a whole is struggling to get people to do the good work, so there’s no shortage of opportunity to bring some of that good work in-house. I don’t know exactly what it is, but I know that we can do it.
“It’s an interesting time. Make the most of it. Let’s strategize. Let’s be proactive. …Let’s not get caught unprepared.”
Featured image: Justin Allen of Hunter Engineering speaks during the 2026 SCRS IDEAS Collide Showcase on Nov. 4. (Lurah Lowery/Repairer Driven News)

articles.title: Understanding Mercedes-Benz TPMS
articles.author: Andrew Markel

paras.en: On different Mercedes-Benz models, you will see two types of TPMS systems. Low-line systems do not display individual tire pressures – these systems just monitor inflation and alert the driver if there is an under-inflation or over-inflation problem with one antenna. Mid-line systems display the individual pressures, and some systems have four antennas mounted near the wheel wells.

Low-line systems can’t detect a low tire pressure until the sensors in the wheels are activated by movement. Mid-line systems can “poke” the sensors with a low-frequency radio signal to get them to transmit information when the vehicle is first started or when prompted by the phone app. But, both systems use the wheel speed sensor to detect a sudden loss of pressure when the vehicle is moving.

Mercedes-Benz and other German vehicle manufacturers make the assumption that people here in the U.S. adjust their tire pressure for the number of people in the vehicle and for the speed they intend to drive. They include the U.S. DOT-mandated tire pressure placard on the driver’s side door jamb, but also behind the gas filler door is the “Luftdruck” sticker, which gives the recommended tire pressure.

This sticker allows the driver set the correct tire pressure for the load and type of driving. If the driver intends to drive at 100 mph with four people in the vehicle, the sticker will advise them to add four more PSI in some cases. This mentality is also part of German tire pressure monitoring systems (TPMS) that require a reference pressure to set during a relearn.

Like all TPMS vehicles, the TPMS light illuminates continuously if one or more of the tires is significantly under or overinflated. If the TPMS light flashes for 60 seconds and then stays illuminated, the TPMS system itself is not operating properly and further diagnostics should be performed. If a condition causing the TPMS to malfunction develops, it may take up to 10 minutes for the system to start flashing a TPMS light.

With almost all Mercedes-Benz vehicles, you should use an auto relearn procedure that is activated by menus in the instrument cluster. The proper menu can vary by model. But, no matter the model or system, always inflate the tires to the recommended pressure before starting any relearn or reset procedure.

When the vehicle is in the restart mode, it is listening for the sensors. During this time, it is looking for the four or five signals that occur on the test drive to determine if a signal is coming from one of the sensors on the vehicle. The tires need to be set at the correct pressure first. This is called the “reference pressure” by Mercedes. If the inflation is not properly set, it could cause the tire pressure alert to come on.

When the restart mode is activated, the display should read, “Tire Pressure Monitor Active,” or “Adopt Current Pressures as New Guidance Values.” Press OK to accept the new values. Or, the display will then issue the message “Use Current Pressures as New Reference Values.” Press OK and then it should show the message, “Tire Press Monitor Restarted.”

Drive the vehicle for at least 10 minutes as the system verifies that the current tire inflation pressures are within the specified range. During the drive, the current tire inflation pressures are accepted as reference values and inflation changes are based on this value.

Mid-line systems will typically require less time to restart or relearn a sensor’s position and start to display pressure values. Low-line systems may require at least 10 minutes of driving to complete the restart.
If a relearn process can’t be completed, use a TPMS tool to activate a sensor to make sure it is active and transmitting. If not, replace the sensor.

articles.title: Understanding the Tesla FSD System
articles.author: Andrew Markel

paras.en: Tesla’s Full Self-Driving (FSD) system can steer, accelerate, brake, change lanes and navigate many roads, but the driver remains responsible for the vehicle. Technicians will need to keep this in mind because a customer report may describe either an expected operating limitation or a condition that needs diagnosis.

System behavior also varies by model, year, hardware and software version. FSD is available on some Cybertruck, Model 3, Model S, Model X, and Model Y vehicles. Always confirm the applicable VIN-specific service information before performing service.

FSD (Supervised) uses the vehicle’s cameras to build a model of the surrounding area. The vehicle’s computer processes that input and uses it to make driving decisions. Depending on the software and vehicle configuration, FSD can follow road curves, respond to traffic lights and stop signs, make turns, change lanes, navigate highway ramps and roundabouts, and follow a route to a destination. The touchscreen displays a visualization of some detected road users and objects, but that display is not a complete representation of every input the system uses.
paras.zh: QUERY LENGTH LIMIT EXCEEDED. MAX ALLOWED QUERY : 500 CHARS

paras.en: The driver can set a destination or allow the vehicle to select a likely route. Speed-profile settings influence speed and lane-change frequency. FSD can be engaged from a stop or while driving, subject to system availability and vehicle conditions. During operation, it may slow for traffic, stop at traffic controls, maneuver around a vehicle partially blocking the lane when space allows, and make lane changes without requiring driver confirmation. The driver can intervene at any time by steering, braking, accelerating or disengaging the system.
paras.zh: QUERY LENGTH LIMIT EXCEEDED. MAX ALLOWED QUERY : 500 CHARS

paras.en: The cabin camera monitors driver attentiveness while FSD is engaged. If the system detects repeated inattention or the driver does not respond to prompts, it can issue escalating warnings and suspend access. Repeated ignored warnings may count as strikeouts and temporarily disable FSD. A driver-initiated disengagement is expected and is not, by itself, improper use.

Before diagnosing a complaint, establish what the vehicle was doing, where it was, the software version, the selected speed profile, the camera and road conditions, and whether the driver received a warning. Confirm that the system was enabled and available, and inspect the touchscreen for messages. Check for clean, unobstructed cameras and current map data. Rain, snow, fog, direct sun, darkness, faded lane markings and camera obstruction can limit performance. A rear-mounted hitch accessory, bike rack or trailer may block a camera or degrade function.
paras.zh: QUERY LENGTH LIMIT EXCEEDED. MAX ALLOWED QUERY : 500 CHARS

paras.en: Some unavailability is expected. FSD may not engage if the driver is not seated with the seat belt fastened, a door or frunk is open, a charge cable is connected, the tailgate is down, or the vehicle is in a mode that restricts the feature. On the Cybertruck, headlights must be set to On or Auto; FSD may disengage or be unavailable if they are Off. A camera obstruction or incomplete calibration can also prevent use.

FSD may need immediate driver intervention on narrow roads, at complex intersections, around construction, during unprotected turns with fast cross traffic, in heavy-traffic merges, near debris, or when road curvature is high. Interactions with pedestrians, cyclists and other road users can also require intervention. The vehicle may brake, steer or change lanes unexpectedly, even when conditions appear straightforward. Visibility is especially important, and poor weather or lighting can significantly degrade performance.
paras.zh: QUERY LENGTH LIMIT EXCEEDED. MAX ALLOWED QUERY : 500 CHARS

paras.en: A complaint that the system is unavailable during one of these conditions may reflect a limitation rather than a failed component. The same may be true if the driver was repeatedly prompted to look at the road, apply slight steering force or take over. If FSD disengages, the driver should receive an alert and chime; determine whether the reported event was a normal disengagement, a warning that went unanswered, or a repeatable fault.

Do not dismiss every report of unexpected behavior as normal. Tesla’s warnings require the driver to supervise, but they do not establish that every maneuver is acceptable. Ask for the exact location, route, road markings, signal state, weather and time of day. Check available vehicle alerts, camera status, calibration state, software and service history. A report of proceeding against a red light, entering an opposing lane or taking a wrong-way turn deserves careful documentation and escalation under applicable service procedures.
paras.zh: QUERY LENGTH LIMIT EXCEEDED. MAX ALLOWED QUERY : 500 CHARS

paras.en: One note: NHTSA opened a preliminary evaluation in October 2025 covering an estimated 2.88 million FSD-equipped vehicles after reports of traffic-law violations, including red-light entry and travel against the proper direction. The agency said it would assess FSD’s ability to detect signals, lane markings and wrong-way signs, along with the warnings and response time provided to drivers. NHTSA notes that an investigation is not a recall determination.
Camera Calibration and the 100-Mile Drive

Camera calibration may be required before some self-driving features are available for the first time or after certain repairs. Cybertruck owner information says calibration usually completes after about 20 to 25 miles, although distance varies with conditions. Clear lane markings, multiple visible lanes, a straight road and light traffic help the process complete. The manual recommends a multi-lane highway, preferably with several lanes and clear markings.

After camera or windshield service, or if a camera has shifted from its calibrated position, the procedure directs the technician to clear calibration through Controls > Service > Camera Calibration > Clear Calibration. The vehicle then repeats its self-calibration process while being driven. Confirm the camera and windshield installation, camera view and relevant service work before the road test; clearing calibration does not correct a physical obstruction or misaligned camera.

Monitor the touchscreen for calibration progress and feature-availability messages. If calibration has not completed after approximately 100 miles driven in suitable conditions, the Cybertruck owner information says to schedule service. Treat 100 miles as the point at which continued failure merits diagnosis. The menu path, conditions and calibration logic can vary by model and software, so verify the procedure for the vehicle being serviced.

Calibration is not a substitute for verifying camera position. If the camera or windshield was replaced, inspect the mounting and optical path and follow the applicable service procedure. A camera that is physically out of specification may repeatedly fail to calibrate or provide unreliable input even after the software calibration has been cleared.

The supplied forward-facing camera pitch procedure is labeled a draft, although it says it has been validated. Confirm the latest procedure and applicability by VIN before starting; do not treat its steps as universal to every Tesla model.

If performing this adjustment on a Cybertruck, the procedure calls for setting ride height to Medium, placing the vehicle in Service Mode, unlocking the Gateway and parking on a flat surface with at least 3.5 feet of clearance in front. Position the camera calibration target against the front fascia, centered on the vehicle, with its bottom 3 feet from the ground. Verify the target is level, then apply red tape at the specified 165-centimeter reference height.

In the touchscreen’s Service Mode, open Driver Assist > Cameras > Camera Preview > Pitch Verification > Main Camera > Wide Camera. Review the main and wide camera images. The top of the tape should align with the blue horizontal line; if it falls between the green lines, pitch is within specification.

If adjustment is required, remove the rearview-mirror beauty cover. The procedure then directs the technician to clear camera calibration, reset DAS and ping DAS using the specified Service Mode Plus functions, followed by adjustment with the pitch-adjustment wrench. Clockwise rotation pitches the camera upward; counterclockwise rotation pitches it downward. Tesla’s procedure states that one rotation can change pitch by approximately 0.5 to 1.5 degrees. Re-check the camera images and repeat the adjustment until the reference falls within the green lines. Reinstall the cover, remove the target, exit Service Mode and complete any required calibration. Use the specified tools and follow the full current procedure, including its safety precautions.
paras.zh: QUERY LENGTH LIMIT EXCEEDED. MAX ALLOWED QUERY : 500 CHARS

paras.en: Two recalls are especially relevant to FSD and camera service. In 2023, recall 23V-085 covered certain Model S, Model X, Model 3 and Model Y vehicles equipped with FSD Beta. The recall addressed certain driving maneuvers that could violate traffic laws or customs; Tesla’s remedy was an over-the-air software update. Recall 23V-489 covered certain 2023 Model S, Model X and Model Y vehicles with forward-facing camera pitch outside specification, which could make certain active-safety features unavailable without alerting the driver. The remedy was inspection and, if needed, pitch adjustment. Check recall status by VIN and confirm completion before diagnosing related complaints.

articles.title: Top 5 Suspension Problems That Shops and DIYers Commonly Misdiagnose
articles.author: TrakMotive

paras.en: Struts, racks, and alignments get blamed for a lot of problems they didn’t cause. In many cases the real cause is a worn chassis part: a sway bar link, a ball joint, a tie rod end, a control arm bushing, or a strut mount. Here are five common misdiagnoses, and how to find the part that’s actually worn.
- A clunk over bumps blamed on struts or shocks

Worn struts usually make a vehicle bouncy or floaty. They rarely clunk. One of the most common sources is a sway bar end link or sway bar bushing, which is a much cheaper part. Worn strut mounts, ball joints, and control arm bushings are also common culprits. A loose exhaust hanger or heat shield can sound like any of them. To find it, grab each end link and try to twist it with the car on the ground. Then have a helper rock the car while you listen and feel at each component.
An alignment that checks out but still pulls is a common source of comebacks. Before you re-align, rule out these causes. Two of them are worn chassis parts:
- Radial tire pull: if swapping the front tires left to right reverses the pull, the tire is the cause.
- A sticking brake caliper: after a drive, one wheel will be noticeably hotter than the other.
- A worn lower control arm bushing: it lets the wheel shift under braking or acceleration.
- A binding strut mount: it causes “memory steer,” where the car pulls in the direction of the last turn.
3. Loose steering or wander blamed on the steering rack

Play at the wheel often comes from somewhere else: a ball joint, control arm bushings, or a worn wheel bearing. How you check matters. Grab the tire at 9 and 3 o’clock and rock it. Play points to tie rods or the rack. Play when you rock it at 12 and 6 points to ball joints or a wheel bearing. Have a helper watch each joint so you can see where the movement actually is. When checking ball joints, remember that a load-carrying joint has to be unloaded before its play will show. If the coil spring sits on the lower control arm, support the lower arm near the joint. On strut designs, lift by the frame. When the spring sits on the upper arm, lift by the frame and wedge a block between the upper arm and the frame. Lifting at the wrong point can hide the wear. If the joint has a wear indicator, use it.
paras.zh: QUERY LENGTH LIMIT EXCEEDED. MAX ALLOWED QUERY : 500 CHARS

paras.en: 4. Tire wear blamed on alignment when the alignment is in spec
The printout is all green, but the tires keep wearing on the inside or feathering. Often the cause is a worn chassis part that the alignment rack can’t detect.

- Bushing deflection: A worn control arm, trailing arm, or subframe bushing can hold correct specs on the alignment rack but still let toe shift under braking, acceleration, or cornering. The rack measures a static car, while the tire wears dynamically. Pry gently on each arm and look for rubber that is cracked, torn, or pushed off center.

- The rear axle gets ignored: Many shops do a front-only alignment on vehicles with adjustable or independent rear suspension. Rear toe or thrust angle that’s off makes the car “dog track,” and the front tires wear while the driver holds a slight steering correction.

- Other factors: Running tires underinflated, carrying heavy loads (which changes camber and toe), skipping rotations, and worn shocks (which cause cupping) all produce wear patterns that look like an alignment problem.
5. Heavy steering or poor return-to-center blamed on the power steering pump, rack, or motor

When steering feels stiff, notchy, or doesn’t straighten itself after a turn, the pump, rack, or electric assist motor usually gets replaced first. Often the real cause is binding in the steering linkage or front suspension, which the power steering system then has to fight. A tie rod end or ball joint costs a fraction of what a new rack does.

- Seized or dry tie rod ends and ball joints. A joint can have no play at all, so it passes a play check, and still be stiff. A stiff joint makes the wheel feel heavy and keeps it from returning to center. Inspectors check for looseness but rarely check for binding. To check, disconnect the joint and move the stud by hand. It should move smoothly, with no notches or tight spots.

- Binding upper strut mount bearings. These cause stiff or notchy steering, often with a creak, pop, or “boing” from the coil spring when turning at low speed. The steering also tends to stay where you leave it after a turn instead of straightening out.

- Low or uneven caster. Caster is the main thing that makes the wheel return to center. A bent control arm or strut tower, a shifted subframe, or a worn radius rod or control arm bushing can reduce it. Uneven caster side to side also causes a pull toward the side with less caster.

Before you replace the strut, the rack, or the alignment, check the chassis. Most of the culprits on this list are worn control arms, ball joints, tie rod ends, sway bar links, bushings, or strut mounts, and Suspensia engineers every one of them to meet or exceed OE specifications.

articles.title: VIPAR Heavy Duty Recaps IMPACT Conference
articles.author: Jeff White

paras.en: The VIPAR Heavy Duty Family of Companies brought its network together for the 2026 IMPACT Conference. A new format encouraged deeper collaboration, generated ideas and aligned distributors, suppliers and business partners around future opportunities. The conference took place in mid-October at the JW Marriott Marco Island in Florida.
VIPAR Heavy Duty Opens Conference with Innovation Focus

Monday’s Distributor Welcome & Kickoff featured entrepreneur, author and speaker Kyle Scheele. His presentation, “Becoming an Idea Factory: How to Build a Culture Where Innovation Is Inevitable,” challenged attendees to rethink problem-solving and leadership. He also discussed creating environments where ideas can thrive.

Scheele encouraged attendees to capture ideas, create trusted processes for developing them and provide room for experimentation. He also urged leaders to protect early concepts from premature dismissal.

“It doesn’t matter what the system is. What matters is that it exists, that your team trusts it, and that ideas put into it can find a home. Your job as a leader is to give your team the goal: here’s the problem, here are the constraints, now bring me ideas,” said Scheele.

That message carried into the rest of the opening day. Distributor roundtables featured discussions about the challenges and opportunities facing independent heavy-duty aftermarket distributors. Attendees explored priorities including technology, data, workforce recruiting, AI, training, order fulfillment and delivery, and parts procurement.

Later, distributors rotated through focus groups where they shared input on group initiatives. Topics included supplier programs, PARTSPHERE innovation, data tools, fleet opportunities and VIPAR Heavy Duty’s partnership with NEXUS Automotive International in Latin America.

For the first time, the conference opened with a day dedicated specifically to distributors. The programming included interactive sessions, roundtable discussions and direct feedback on priorities affecting independent distributors and the broader heavy-duty aftermarket.

On day two, the format expanded to include distributors, suppliers, business partners and associates. The first shared general session brought the entire network together to hear organizational priorities and discuss opportunities for closer collaboration.

Leaders emphasized that each part of the network brings a different perspective. They also discussed how connecting those viewpoints can produce better insights, stronger relationships and new opportunities.
“The strength of this network is not found in any one company. It is created when all of our perspectives come together,” said Jeff Paul, executive vice president.
Network Leaders Outline Growth Priorities

General session presentations highlighted several strategic priorities for continued growth. These included expansion across the Americas, stronger supplier engagement and continued investment in training and product information.
Other priorities included technology, responsible data sharing, expanded sales channels and a renewed focus on fleets and end users.

Chris Baer, president and CEO of the VIPAR Heavy Duty Family of Companies, outlined a regional approach to network development. His strategy covers the United States, Canada, Mexico and Latin America. Baer emphasized finding the right partners for sustainable growth rather than simply expanding distribution.
“Our next stage of growth will come from strong partners, bold ideas, and the discipline to turn those ideas into results,” said Baer.

The week also included IMPACT Conference traditions such as the trade show, scheduled one-on-one distributor-supplier meetings and networking activities. These events provided additional opportunities to discuss products, business priorities and potential partnerships.
Alex Rodriguez Shares Leadership Lessons
Thursday’s keynote featured Alex Rodriguez, who drew on his baseball career, business ventures and personal experiences. He discussed preparation, humility, accountability and continuous learning.
Rodriguez connected building a winning sports team with developing a successful organization. He emphasized the importance of clear vision, capable people and alignment around shared goals.
He also challenged leaders to recognize their blind spots and remain accountable for mistakes. Rodriguez encouraged them to embrace learning when entering unfamiliar fields.

“There’s no greater investment than investing in yourself,” said Rodriguez, encouraging them to continue developing their communication, writing, and other skills and to keep learning throughout their careers.
Conference Sets Stage for Future Collaboration
Throughout the 2026 IMPACT Conference, participants emphasized the value of sharing knowledge, developing ideas and pursuing common opportunities.

The VIPAR Heavy Duty Family of Companies plans to continue developing programs and supporting independent distributors and supplier partners. The organization also intends to build on its collaborative approach as it prepares for future growth.
The 2027 VIPAR Heavy Duty Family of Companies IMPACT Conference will take place Oct. 17-22 at the JW Marriott Orlando Grande Lakes in Orlando, Florida.

articles.title: Celebrating the Women Who Move Our Industry Forward
articles.author: Brandi Gangel

paras.en: There are plenty of reasons to love AAPEX. The innovation, the energy, the business opportunities, and of course, the people. Wednesday morning’s breakfast, the kickoff to Wednesday, Women in Auto Care offered a particularly meaningful reminder of what makes the automotive aftermarket such a special industry to be part of.

The Women in Auto Care Annual Networking Breakfast and Awards program brought together an incredible community of industry professionals to celebrate the women making a difference in our businesses, our industry, and in the lives of those around them.

Throughout the morning, as award recipients took the stage, a common theme emerged. Despite their different career paths, experiences, and accomplishments, nearly every woman spoke about the same thing: the people who helped them get where they are today.

The mentors who saw potential before they saw it in themselves. The colleagues who became lifelong friends. The families who supported big dreams, long hours, and bold decisions. And the women who opened doors, offered encouragement, and made room for others at the table. It was a powerful reminder that while individual accomplishments deserve to be celebrated, very few of us get where we are entirely on our own.

One particularly touching moment came from a young award recipient who spoke about her three-year-old daughter growing up surrounded by strong women in automotive. To her daughter, the industry isn’t male dominated, it’s simply a place where her mom, her grandmother, and countless other women belong, contribute, and succeed. What an incredible perspective. And what a wonderful reflection of the progress this organization continues to make.

Another recipient shared the story of her grandmother, who helped operate a family service station decades ago but was overlooked when the business received industry recognition. Generations later, today, her granddaughter stood on stage accepting a Shop Owner of the Year Award, dedicating the honor to the woman who helped inspire her.

And in a memorable moment of audience participation, another honoree distributed tiny pink army women, encouraging attendees to keep one as a reminder of their own strength and give another to someone who could use a little encouragement. A simple gesture with a powerful message: We all have an army behind us, and we have an opportunity to be part of someone else’s.

These stories were different, but their message was remarkably consistent. Success isn’t only measured by titles, accomplishments, or recognition, it’s also measured by the opportunities we create, the relationships we build, and the people we help along the way. That’s what makes Women in Auto Care so special.

It has built a community where women genuinely celebrate one another’s successes, encourage each other’s ambitions, and invest in the next generation of leaders. A big congratulations to all this year’s award winners and finalists. And to the Women in Auto Care organization, its leadership, volunteers, allies and supporters, thank you for creating opportunities to recognize women and champion their contributions to our industry.

articles.title: Parts Authority Announces 2026 Vendor Partner Awards
articles.author: Mary DellaValle

paras.en: Parts Authority, distributor of automotive replacement parts, tools and equipment, announced the winners of its 2026 vendor awards at AWDA/AAPEX Industry Week. The awards honor the suppliers and representatives whose work over the past year did the most to move the business forward.

“Every one of these partners helped us serve our customers better this year,” said Clark Hale, CEO of Parts Authority. “We are grateful for the effort, reliability, and trust behind these results, and we congratulate everyone recognized.”
Supplier of the Year: SKF. Parts Authority’s top vendor honor went to SKF for its outstanding overall contribution and the strength of its partnership across the year.
Import Supplier of the Year: Bosch. Bosch was recognized for delivering the quality products and dependable support that Parts Authority’s import customers count on.
Partnership Award: DRiV. DRiV was elected for broad strategic synergy and continuous multi-category collaboration across product lines.
Supply Chain Award: Deka. Deka was honored for keeping product moving with consistency and dependability, a key factor in meeting customer demand.
Marketing Excellence Award: Dorman. Recognized for creative installer engagement, high-impact technician education, and targeted merchandising programs that accelerated new-to-market part adoption.
Catalog and Data Award: Mevotech. Mevotech was recognized for the quality of its product data, including accurate listings and rich content that make parts easier to find and sell.
Brand Recognition Award: Gates. Gates received this award for a brand reputation built on quality and trust that continues to resonate with customers.
New Vendor Award: Sylvania. Sylvania was welcomed with this inaugural recognition for making a strong first impression as a new Parts Authority partner.

Vendor Representative of the Year: Parts Authority named two honorees this year, Norman Charleville of Premium Guard and George Greene of Arnott Industries, for their dependable support and their role in strengthening the relationship between their companies and Parts Authority.

Manufacturer Representative of the Year: Jim Guy of NA Williams and Hector Garcia of Stan Padover Associates, Inc. were recognized for their teamwork, their skill in balancing multi-line portfolios, supporting regional inventory initiatives, and strengthening branch-level vendor relationships.
The Road Warrior Award recognizes representatives who go the extra mile for customers and colleagues. This year’s recipients are:
- Justin Masseo, Glazier Sales Associates
- William Shost, Glazier Sales Associates
“These individuals show up, stay engaged, and make a difference every day,” said Hale. “We are proud to call them partners.”

articles.title: Bo Fisher Receives 2026 AWDA Lifetime Achievement Award
articles.author: Mary DellaValle

paras.en: The Aftermarket Warehouse Distributors Association (AWDA), a community of the Auto Care Association, presented its 2026 Lifetime Achievement Award in honor of Martin Fromm to Bo Fisher, Chairman and CEO of Fisher Auto Parts. The award was presented by AWDA Chairperson Fletcher Lord III on November 1 at AWDA’s 2026 Annual Conference in Las Vegas.

AWDA’s Lifetime Achievement Award recognizes individuals who have, over the course of many years, distinguished themselves through their unselfish commitment to, and high level of performance within, the motor vehicle aftermarket industry. The award is named in honor of former AWDA President Martin Fromm.

As chairman and CEO of Fisher Auto Parts, Fisher has built upon a remarkable family legacy while leading one of the industry’s most respected independent distribution organizations. Under his leadership, the company expanded to approximately 500 company-owned locations and many more independent locations across 18 states, achieving tenfold growth over two decades while remaining debt-free.

Fisher has championed collaboration among independent distributors and built an organization grounded in relationships, customer service, integrity and commitment to the professional automotive service industry. His dedication to education continues the vision of his father, Art Fisher, through the Art Fisher Memorial Scholarship program, annual scholarships and the KOI/Fisher Training Cavalcade. His contributions earned him the Mort Schwartz Excellence in Education Award.

Throughout his career, Fisher has demonstrated humility, loyalty, generosity and a willingness to share knowledge and opportunity. His legacy extends beyond the company he has grown to the industry he has strengthened, the people he has inspired and the opportunities he has created.

articles.title: The Case for Fewer SKUs
articles.author: Jeff White

paras.en: Every automotive parts store faces the same inventory challenge: having the right parts available without tying up too much capital. With thousands of SKUs competing for limited shelf space, finding the right balance isn’t easy.
Bill Nunnery, senior director, sales and marketing, Global Aftermarket at Dana Incorporated, believes SKU consolidation can help stores address that challenge while improving customer service.
“The one challenge that every distributor is faced with is having the right part at the right place at the right time,” Nunnery said.
Inventory management involves more than keeping shelves stocked. Stores must also consider how much working capital they invest in inventory and whether those products generate sufficient sales.

Nunnery said the industry has little tolerance for slow-moving inventory, particularly as shelf space becomes increasingly valuable. Carrying similar products from multiple suppliers can further complicate inventory management. Reducing redundant SKUs can help stores control costs while simplifying the purchasing process.
“And so minimizing the complexity and choices is always a good thing for the customer,” Nunnery said.
That means fewer overlapping options to navigate while helping customers identify the appropriate products for their applications.

Counter pros see firsthand which products customers request most often and which alternatives can serve multiple applications. That experience can provide valuable insight into inventory decisions, particularly when stores evaluate overlapping products or identify opportunities to simplify their assortments.
Nunnery pointed to Dana’s Reinzosil universal sealing compound as an example of how SKU consolidation can benefit parts stores and repair shops.

According to Nunnery, one tube of Reinzosil can replace 10 to 12 conventional RTV sealant varieties. That allows distributors to reduce inventory requirements while offering a product that serves multiple applications.

The benefits extend into the repair bay. A technician might otherwise keep 10 or 12 different tubes of RTV sealant in a toolbox. Those tubes take up space, and their contents have a limited shelf life.
“You’ve got to remember this is a perishable item,” Nunnery said.

Consolidating those products into one sensor-safe solution can simplify inventory management for technicians while reducing the number of individual products they must purchase and maintain. The same principle applies at the parts store.

Nunnery noted that an automotive retailer or independent parts store might dedicate 10 to 12 linear feet of shelf space to RTV products. He estimated that consolidating the category around a universal solution could reduce merchandising requirements by 70% to 80%. That would free valuable space for other products without requiring additional shelving or warehouse capacity.

Of course, reducing SKUs shouldn’t come at the expense of product availability or application coverage. Nunnery emphasized that distributors must evaluate consolidation opportunities with their customers’ needs in mind.
“I think when they’re deciding on consolidation, I think it always, again, it starts with the customer first,” he said.

That philosophy should guide inventory decisions throughout the distribution chain. Manufacturers and distributors can use category management analytics to identify opportunities to reduce inventory while maintaining appropriate application coverage.

Ultimately, successful SKU consolidation requires collaboration between manufacturers and distributors. The objective isn’t simply to stock fewer products. It’s to reduce unnecessary complexity, make better use of available resources and ensure customers can get the products they need.
For parts stores, that’s a strategy that can benefit both sides of the counter.

articles.title: 50% of long COVID patients show improvement in 3 years — but the condition tends to linger in those with this subtype
articles.author: RJ Mackenzie

paras.en: Symptoms of long COVID ease in half of patients within three years of the infection that kicked off their illness.

That's the primary conclusion of a new study that tracked over 1,000 patients with long COVID, a chronic condition that can emerge after an infection with the SARS-CoV-2 virus. Among the patients, the chance of improvement varied sharply depending on how the condition affected their bodily systems.

In the study, published Tuesday (Nov. 3) in the journal Annals of Internal Medicine, roughly 60% of patients whose predominant symptoms were changes to their ability to taste or smell had significantly improved three years after their first positive test. But less than 20% of those with a multisystem presentation had improved in that time frame.

This latter group had symptoms that affected their cardiac, nervous and gastrointestinal systems, among others. An expert told Live Science that the condition resembled myalgic encephalomyelitis/chronic fatigue syndrome (ME/CFS), which often arises after an infection and similarly impacts a wide range of bodily systems.
The new study's findings could help direct the structure of future clinical trials of treatments for long COVID, experts said.

The patients in the study were enrolled in the long-term RECOVER Adult Study. Funded by the National Institutes of Health, the project has recruited thousands of adults across the United States who previously tested positive for COVID-19.

Researchers scored patients based on how they were affected by a range of symptoms, including fatigue, brain fog, shortness of breath and heart palpitations. The study included patients who scored more than 10 points on a 30-point scale — called the 2024 LC Research Index (LCRI) — which attempted to capture these different symptom combinations.
Get the world’s most fascinating discoveries delivered straight to your inbox.

Nearly 1,020 patients met this requirement and were tracked over time; they had in-person appointments and filled out symptom surveys every three months. Scientists marked patients as "improved" once they recorded LCRI scores of 10 or less at two consecutive visits. They found that 36% of the participants had improved two years after their inciting COVID-19 infection, and that figure rose to 50% after three years.
LCRIs hit zero for 26% of the participants after three years, meaning all of their symptoms were gone at the time of the survey.

Reeder said he was careful to avoid describing the participants as "recovered." This decision was influenced by input from the long COVID community to the RECOVER Adult Study, he said. They highlighted that their symptoms can wax and wane, whereas "recovery" implies a permanent resolution. The new study didn't capture, for example, whether individual patients who recorded meaningful improvement later relapsed.

Some patients' journeys were far less straightforward than the top-line data might suggest. Although men and women improved at similar rates, adults under 46 were more likely to improve than older participants were. Patients affected by the Omicron variants of SARS-CoV-2, which emerged in 2021 and quickly became the dominant strain of the virus, were more likely to improve than those infected with earlier strains.
Some of the starkest differences in improvement rates were seen between patients with different symptoms.
In a previous study, RECOVER researchers had grouped participants into five subtypes, using an algorithm to connect patients with similar predominant symptoms:
- Symptoms affecting multiple bodily systems
In the new study, patients in the last three groups were less likely to get better within three years. The final group's rate was particularly low, at just 19%.
Dr. Carmen Scheibenbogen, an immunologist at Charité University Medicine Berlin, said these patients' progress resembles that of people with ME/CFS.

"It looks as if at least a major subgroup is suffering from ME-CFS," Scheibenbogen said, noting that COVID-19 may have triggered their condition. "This is a disease which is triggered by different infections, but in the end, the disease [itself] is very similar," she said.
Like long COVID, ME/CFS can affect a wide array of bodily systems, and it remains poorly understood despite recent advances in research.

The team's new findings highlight the need for clinical trials to test possible treatments for long COVID. Both Scheibenbogen and study co-author Harrison Reeder, a biostatistician at Massachusetts General Hospital, said these subtypes would be important to consider in the design of these potential trials.

The multisystem subgroup, Reeder said, "might be a group where an effective intervention can make a bigger difference than people who stand to potentially have a higher chance of improvement regardless."
Future work would need to further scientists' understanding of people affected by long COVID at the level of their genes and proteins, both scientists said.
"There's a lot of work to do in RECOVER and in the world of long COVID research," Harrison said. "There's a lot of opportunity."
This article is for informational purposes only and is not meant to offer medical advice.

RJ Mackenzie is an award-nominated science and health journalist. He has degrees in neuroscience from the University of Edinburgh and the University of Cambridge. He became a writer after deciding that the best way of contributing to science would be from behind a keyboard rather than a lab bench. He has reported on everything from brain-interface technology to shape-shifting materials science, and from the rise of predatory conferencing to the importance of newborn-screening programs. He is a former staff writer of Technology Networks.

articles.title: Perfectly preserved owl fossil from 47 million years ago could help to solve a major evolutionary mystery
articles.author: Sascha Pare

paras.en: A fledgling owl that lived 47 million years ago in what is now Germany offers tantalizing new clues about when most of these birds became nocturnal, a new study shows. The discovery brings researchers one step closer to finally solving the biggest mystery about these birds.

The young owl is a newly described species named Masillastrix blattophaga. Researchers unearthed the almost perfectly preserved bird in 2025 in the Messel Pit, an ancient lake surrounded by a forest that is now the richest fossil site in the world for understanding life in the Eocene epoch (56 million to 34 million years ago). The skull is missing, but the rest of the fossil was so well preserved that researchers found the owl's last meal in its stomach: a greenish-blue, iridescent cockroach.

The cockroach is one of several pieces of evidence suggesting that this tiny owl was diurnal, or active primarily during the day. Iridescence is associated with a diurnal lifestyle, so it appears that the owl, which measured less than 5 inches (12 centimeters) long, was hunting in the daytime, researchers said in the new study.

This indicates that owls were not nocturnal 47 million years ago and so must have switched to the night-owl lifestyle more recently, said study first author Gerald Mayr, a paleontologist and head of ornithology at the Senckenberg Research Institute and the Natural History Museum Frankfurt in Germany.

"There exists a consensus that owls must have evolved from a diurnal ancestor," Mayr told Live Science in an email. That's because some early owl fossils have head-rotation structures similar to those of diurnal raptors and bony ridges above the eye sockets that could have shaded the owls' eyes from the sun.

Therefore, it is plausible that the Messel owl was fully diurnal, rather than active during the daytime and nighttime as some owls are today, because that would imply that some of its ancestors had already evolved nocturnal traits, Mayr said.

Researchers also found a cockroach identical to the one in the Messel owl's stomach in sediments just a few feet away from the new fossil. This well-preserved cockroach helped the team to identify the insect inside the owl, the researchers wrote in the study, which was published Nov. 2 in the journal Current Biology.
Get the world’s most fascinating discoveries delivered straight to your inbox.

It's possible that the owl ate the cockroach at dawn or at dusk, which might cast doubt on whether the bird was diurnal. But there are other clues hinting that the owl was diurnal, including the appearance of some of the owl's feathers and the stoutness of its upper wing bones.

Mayr said he and his colleagues believe the shape of the upper wing bones, or humeri, is an indicator of when owls are active. The Messel owl's stocky humeri hint that the species flew during the day, when silent movement doesn't confer a significant advantage because there is enough light to see predators. Conversely, modern nocturnal owls have slim humeri and fly almost soundlessly, he said.

Assuming this hypothesis is correct, the earliest known nocturnal owl species are from about 35 million years ago, in the Late Eocene, Mayr said. Owl fossils from this period and more recently look a lot like modern owls and have elongated humeri, he noted. The oldest known owl in the fossil record, Ogygoptynx wetmorei, dates to around 60 million years ago.

This means that owls likely became nocturnal between 47 million and 35 million years ago. This is the best current estimate, because the owl fossil record is very sparse and species are often described from only a few isolated bones, according to the study.
"We still know so little about the early evolution of modern birds," Mayr said, adding that every fossil discovery has the power to change even well-established ideas in the field.
- 'I'm more hopeful that birds can endure than maybe even our own species': Paleontologist Steve Brusatte on why birds are the ultimate survivors
- 'He began to cry, and almost fell to the floor': The fluffy fossil that finally showed the world that birds are dinosaurs
- Ancient duck-like creature discovered in Antarctica may be the oldest modern bird ever discovered

The big question that remains is why owls became nocturnal. Previous theories suggested that owls evolved this behavior to avoid competition with diurnal birds of prey or to benefit from a proliferation of nocturnal mammals. But studies show that both of these groups exploded much later than 35 million years ago — around 20 million to 25 million years ago — suggesting there wasn't a clear advantage driving owls to switch to nocturnal lifestyles at that time.

The new results have deepened the uncertainty of why owls turned nocturnal. But "by narrowing down the time frame when owls became nocturnal, our study may eventually contribute to solving this mystery," Mayr said.

Sascha is a U.K.-based staff writer at Live Science. She holds a bachelor’s degree in biology from the University of Southampton in England and a master’s degree in science communication from Imperial College London. Her work has appeared in The Guardian and the health website Zoe. Besides writing, she enjoys playing tennis, bread-making and browsing second-hand shops for hidden gems.

articles.title: How frequently did Viking women fight in battle?
articles.author: Owen Jarus

paras.en: The Vikings were explorers, farmers, merchants and, most famously, warriors who launched raids across large parts of Europe.

Stereotypes of Vikings usually conjure up images of muscular men. But over the past few decades, researchers have turned their attention to women of the Viking Age (roughly A.D. 793 to 1066) and the roles they held. For instance, there are stories of "shield maidens" who fought alongside men, and some of these texts mention Viking women who fought in battle. The archaeological record also holds evidence, including graves of Viking Age women who were buried with war-grade weapons and shields.

It's still a matter of debate whether women who lived during the Viking Age could be warriors, but this discussion raises another question: It's one thing to have texts describing female fighters and archaeological records of women buried with weapons, but what can the evidence tell us about how frequently Viking women fought in battle?

The answer, experts told Live Science, largely depends on our interpretation of texts, artifacts, and burials of Viking Age women, which often face higher scrutiny than burials of men who were buried with similar (or even fewer) weapons.

The Vikings used a runic system of writing, but they left precious few texts behind. Instead, much of what we know about the Vikings was written about them by people from other cultures or by their Norse descendants.

One of the most evocative texts was written in the 12th century by the Danish historian and theologian Saxo Grammaticus. In "Gesta Danorum" (Latin for "History of the Danes" and translated by Jenny Jochens), he wrote that "there were once women in Denmark who dressed themselves to look like men and spent almost every minute cultivating [combat] skills." As "if they were forgetful of their true selves they put toughness before allure, aimed at conflicts instead of kisses, tasted blood, not lips, sought the clash of arms rather than the arm's embrace, fitted to weapons hands what should have been weaving, desired not the couch but the kill, and those they could have appeased with looks they attacked with lances."
paras.zh: QUERY LENGTH LIMIT EXCEEDED. MAX ALLOWED QUERY : 500 CHARS

paras.en: Another text about the Vikings, the medieval Irish "Cogadh Gaedhelre Gallaibh" ("War of the Irish with the Foreigners"), refers to a woman known as the "Red Lady" leading a Viking fleet in a raid on Belfast in the 10th century.
Feed your curiosity with an exclusive mystery every week, solved with science and delivered direct to your inbox before it's seen anywhere else.

There's a lot of uncertainty, said Neil Price, an archaeology professor at Uppsala University in Sweden who has written extensively about the Vikings. The text in the "Cogadh Gaedhel re Gallaibh" that refers to the Red Lady is of debatable accuracy, Price told Live Science in an email.
He suspects that Viking women fought in battle but not frequently. In addition, "female warriors were probably a very small minority," Price said.
The account written by Saxo Grammaticus is also contentious. Thomas Kristian Heebøll-Holm, a history professor at the University of Southern Denmark, said Saxo Grammaticus is not a reliable source.

"Saxo Grammaticus does write about female warriors, but only in the parts of his work concerned [with] the legendary past of Denmark," Heebøll-Holm told Live Science in an email. "Furthermore, these writings are not accurate, but moral and fictitious," Heebøll-Holm said, noting that, in some instances, Saxo Grammaticus seemed to be drawing on the stories of the Amazons, a group of legendary female warriors whom the ancient Greeks believed in with stories about them dating back more than 2,500 years.
paras.zh: QUERY LENGTH LIMIT EXCEEDED. MAX ALLOWED QUERY : 500 CHARS

paras.en: Archaeological evidence can also be challenging to interpret. Archaeologists know of about 30 Viking Age female burials containing weapons, including three with swords in Scandinavia. Even more Viking Age women's graves have items that could have been used as weapons — including spears, axes and knives — although these tools also could have been used for hunting or tending to farms. Either way, we can't be sure if these women fought in battle.

"The first concern is that the weapons were really used by the deceased and were not merely included as signs of special status or social rank acquired through inheritance," Deborah Shepherd, an independent researcher who holds a doctorate in archaeology and has studied the Vikings extensively, told Live Science in an email. She noted that graves are often not well preserved, making it difficult to gather information.

There were likely "some few female warriors, but they were probably only found in the highest ranking families, and their warrior career was probably short-lived," Shepherd said. "They wouldn't have fought in the great armies of later centuries but possibly did fight in pre-Christian skirmishes." (The Vikings began gradually converting to Christianity between the ninth and 12th centuries.)

There is at least one known case of a Viking woman found with what may be combat-related injuries. A Viking woman found in Solør, Norway, had a head injury consistent with a sword strike. She was 18 or 19 at the time she died, was buried with weapons and lived around 900.
Ole Kastholm, a curator and senior researcher at the Roskilde Museum in Denmark, said there is a lot of uncertainty regarding how frequently Viking Age women fought in battle.

Weapons "do occur as a grave good in a handful of graves with female human remains," Kastholm told Live Science in an email. "Often it is just a single weapon [such] as a spear or [a] battle axe. But we know of at least one example of a female grave with a full set of weapons as well as riding equipment," which is located in Birka, Sweden.
"If this was a man's grave, researchers would have no doubt that it was a warrior grave, and this explanation must necessarily also apply when the interred is a woman," Kastholm said.

That said, there were female warriors in other cultures. "One can also note in passing that female warriors were an almost common feature of central Asian societies for at least a millennium before the Viking Age," Price wrote in his book, "The Sea-King and the Sorceress: Life and Death in the Viking Age" (Basic Books, 2026).

For instance the Scythians are a people who flourished in eastern Europe and Asia and Scythian women have been found buried with horses and weapons. In some cases, the Scythian women suffered combat wounds such as arrowheads and it's been speculated that they may have been an inspiration for stories of the Amazons.
See how much you know about ancient norsemen with our Viking quiz!

Owen Jarus is a regular contributor to Live Science who writes about archaeology and humans' past. He has also written for The Independent (UK), The Canadian Press (CP) and The Associated Press (AP), among others. Owen has a bachelor of arts degree from the University of Toronto and a journalism degree from Ryerson University.
