articles.title: 2,800-year-old tomb in Siberia has evidence of the earliest use of cannabis — possibly as a way to calm human sacrifice victims
articles.author: Kristina Killgrove

paras.en: Archaeologists have unearthed the oldest evidence of cannabis use from a 2,800-year-old monumental tomb in Siberia. The presence of plant seeds in the grave and chemical traces of the drug in mummy hair suggest people practiced a funeral ritual that may have involved a grim practice: calming human sacrifice victims with cannabis.

In a study published Thursday (Nov. 5) in the journal Science, researchers investigated the contents of a "royal mound" burial at the Tunnug archaeological site in the Uyuk valley of southern Siberia. Archaeologists discovered four wooden structures containing several log coffins in the middle of the mound. On top of the wooden burial structures were the skeletons of horses that once formed a "spectral cavalcade," a Scythian funeral tradition that involved sacrificing horses and humans. And inside the burial structures, the archaeologists discovered piles of tiny seeds from the plant Cannabis ruderalis, a wild type of cannabis or marijuana.
paras.zh: QUERY LENGTH LIMIT EXCEEDED. MAX ALLOWED QUERY : 500 CHARS

paras.en: Cannabis likely originated in Asia and was cultivated thousands of years ago for various purposes, including for ropes and textiles, and 6,000 years ago as an oilseed crop, according to the study. But it's unclear when people learned about the psychoactive properties of the plant. In the fifth century B.C., the ancient Greek historian Herodotus wrote that the Scythian nomads inhaled the fumes from burning hemp seeds. And evidence of cannabis use was previously discovered in a cemetery in China dated to about 500 B.C. The new study, however, pushes back this date by three centuries.
paras.zh: QUERY LENGTH LIMIT EXCEEDED. MAX ALLOWED QUERY : 500 CHARS

paras.en: Researchers discovered more than 1,000 whole cannabis seeds and around 500 partial seeds in the Tunnug burial mound, and they carbon-dated them to between 800 and 760 B.C. They also recovered several human hair samples from the grave. An analysis of the hair revealed signals matching cannabinol and THC (tetrahydrocannabinol), psychoactive chemical compounds found in cannabis. The tests could not determine how much of the drug people consumed, however.

"The molecular traces in the hair and the cannabis seeds come from the same grave and suggest that cannabis was used for its intoxicating properties," study first author Gino Caspari, an archaeologist at the Max Planck Institute of Geoanthropology in Jena, Germany, said in a statement.
But given the burial context of the discovery, the use of cannabis may have had a darker purpose.

"In this princely tomb, the burials were accompanied by extensive horse sacrifices and, most likely, human sacrifices as well," Caspari said. The tradition of human sacrifice, in particular, "would have potentially made the plant a useful agent to calm individuals who were to be included in the rituals," the researchers wrote in the study.
Get the world’s most fascinating discoveries delivered straight to your inbox.

The new study confirms the ancient use of cannabis in funerals in Central Asia and extends the date back to 2,800 years ago, the researchers noted. Future work is planned but will focus on other aspects of ancient cannabis.
"We have already begun sequencing some of the plant samples," Caspari said. "This will help us learn more about the history of the domestication and spread of the crop soon."

Kristina Killgrove is a staff writer at Live Science with a focus on archaeology and paleoanthropology news. Her articles have also appeared in venues such as Forbes, Smithsonian, and Mental Floss. Kristina holds a Ph.D. in biological anthropology and an M.A. in classical archaeology from the University of North Carolina, as well as a B.A. in Latin from the University of Virginia, and she was formerly a university professor and researcher. She has received awards from the Society for American Archaeology and the American Anthropological Association for her science writing.

articles.title: Why do most cats hate it when you touch their belly, feet or tail?
articles.author: Clarissa Brincat

paras.en: Dogs typically love belly rubs and will roll on their backs to get more. With cats, it's a different story: Most are visibly uncomfortable when someone touches their belly, and the same applies to their feet and tail.

When a cat is petted in these areas, its body language often changes. "They might do a quick head turn, looking at your hand, or they might start moving away from you or wiggling around a lot, basically trying to get away from the petting," Mikel Delgado, a cat behaviorist and senior research scientist at Purdue University, told Live Science in an email. "If these early warning signs are ignored, they might escalate to biting, hissing or scratching."
But why do cats dislike it so much when humans touch these specific areas?
Although there has been little formal research into this question, animal behavior experts proposed a few ideas for why cats don't like to be touched in certain areas.

"Cats are prey animals as well as predators and so they can be very protective of areas that are particularly vulnerable to injury during attack, such as the belly area," Sarah Ellis, head of cat mental well-being and behavior at the cat welfare charity International Cat Care, told Live Science in an email.

A cat's belly houses vital organs — such as the liver, stomach and intestines — without the protective bony cage that the ribs provide for the heart and lungs. Although cats have evolved a special feature called the "primordial pouch" — basically a flap of loose skin and fat on their belly — which provides a little extra padding to protect vital organs during fights, most cats still feel threatened when humans touch or rub their belly.

Dogs have a similar anatomy to cats, but they have to worry less about falling prey to larger animals. Cats, meanwhile, can be hunted by dogs, urban coyotes, and even birds such as hawks and owls, making it natural for them to be protective of their bellies.
Feed your curiosity with an exclusive mystery every week, solved with science and delivered direct to your inbox before it's seen anywhere else.

The tail is also a vulnerable area for cats. "When a cat is chased by another animal, including other cats, the tail is often the part of the cat's body that is closest to touch," Ellis said, "and the risk of being bitten at the base of the tail is high." Therefore, cats may be skittish about having their tail stroked.

When it comes to foot rubs, there are two possible explanations for why most cats hate them. First, a cat's paws are essential in threatening situations. Running away from danger is a cat's preferred survival strategy, and they rely on their paws as a means of escape, Ellis explained. If they can't run away, "a cat may resort to repelling any threats through swiping and scratching and it needs its paws free to do so," she said. "It is therefore predisposed to not enjoy having its paws restricted in any way."
paras.zh: QUERY LENGTH LIMIT EXCEEDED. MAX ALLOWED QUERY : 500 CHARS

paras.en: Another reason could be that cats' paws are very sensitive. They have wrist whiskers (also known as "carpal vibrissae") and toe pads that are sensitive to various types of stimuli, like pressure and heat, Delgado said, "so it's not surprising that many cats are sensitive about having their feet touched."

If you're interacting with a cat, it's generally a good idea to stick to the areas where most cats like to be petted: the base of their ears, around their cheeks and under their chin. These areas are rich in scent glands, and cats tend to rub them against other cats they are friends with, Delgado explained. So essentially, cats like being petted in those areas because "they treat us as they do other cats," Delgado said.

But some cats go against the grain. "I've had a few who enjoyed belly rubs," Delgado said. Others enjoy having their tail stroked briefly and show their pleasure "by pushing their rump into the hand of the petter and holding their tail up in the air," Ellis said. (This behavior is sometimes called "elevator butt.")

As puzzling as it may be to humans, these varied preferences are a reminder that "each cat is an individual," Delgado said. Positive responses to petting of the belly, feet or tail can also signal close bonding to a human, Ellis said.
She advises people to "always take the cat's lead, learn what each individual cat likes and dislikes and respect these preferences."

Clarissa Brincat is a freelance writer specializing in health and medical research. After completing an MSc in chemistry, she realized she would rather write about science than do it. She learned how to edit scientific papers in a stint as a chemistry copyeditor, before moving on to a medical writer role at a healthcare company. Writing for doctors and experts has its rewards, but Clarissa wanted to communicate with a wider audience, which naturally led her to freelance health and science writing. articles.title: I almost died from flu. My life didn't go back to normal after.
articles.author: Hannah Osborne

paras.en: In February 2011, Madi Allen, a healthy 12-year-old in Central Illinois, who loved playing sports, almost died from the flu. The influenza B virus resulted in her developing necrotizing pneumonia, where the infection triggers inflammation that destroys the tissue of the lungs, methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus (MRSA), and her kidneys shut down. She was put on life support and dialysis, and was intubated for five weeks. She spent another two months in hospital and a decade recovering from the damage caused.
paras.zh: QUERY LENGTH LIMIT EXCEEDED. MAX ALLOWED QUERY : 500 CHARS

paras.en: Allen, now 28, shared her experience with Live Science.
I was 12 years old when it all started. I was just a normal seventh grader, I played soccer and basketball. I didn't really have any health issues beforehand — just sports-induced asthma.

That weekend, I started to feel a little sick, but nothing too bad. My mom kept giving me over-the-counter medicine and it would work for a bit, then once it wore off, it would get really bad. I'd planned to go to one of my friend's birthday parties then spend the night with my best friend. I went to the party, but I texted my mom saying I should come home because I really wasn't feeling well, which was not usual for me at all. That night I asked my mom to sleep with me because I just felt terrible.
paras.zh: QUERY LENGTH LIMIT EXCEEDED. MAX ALLOWED QUERY : 500 CHARS

paras.en: That was Saturday. By Sunday night, the only position that I could get comfortable in was my mom holding me like a baby. My mom just held me all weekend. My whole body just hurt and I started feeling like I couldn't breathe properly. That got way worse Monday morning.

We were waiting for my pediatrician to open up and my mom suggested taking a shower, saying, "Maybe that will help you feel a bit better before we go to the doctor." She had to help me take a shower because I was so weak, I couldn't stand by myself. She stepped away for a second just to grab a towel and said that when she came back, my lips were turning gray and my eyes were starting to look sunken in. She knew that something was not right so she called my dad, who was at the grocery store, and told him to just leave everything, that we need to get to the hospital.
paras.zh: QUERY LENGTH LIMIT EXCEEDED. MAX ALLOWED QUERY : 500 CHARS

paras.en: Our local hospital is just a small rural hospital — everybody gets transferred out. They diagnosed me with double pneumonia and then sent me to a different hospital 30 minutes away that specialized more in kids.

My dad rode with me in the ambulance while my mom went home and grabbed a few things — she thought we'd just be there for a few days. By the time we got to the second hospital, I was in respiratory distress. They wanted to intubate me straight away but were waiting until my mom got there so she could talk to me — my dad did the best he could, but my dad didn't know how to calm me down.

I don't think the doctors even told me that they were putting me to sleep. My mom had to be the one to tell me. I remember being very scared. They put this mask on my face for the BiPAP [bilevel positive airway pressure machine, which delivers pressurized air to a patient] and I felt like that was suffocating me. It didn't feel like it was helping at all, which, I guess, at that point, it wasn't. They were just trying everything they could. I was begging them to take it off of me, crying and just saying, "one minute, just take it off for one minute."
paras.zh: QUERY LENGTH LIMIT EXCEEDED. MAX ALLOWED QUERY : 500 CHARS

paras.en: Finally my mom tried to calm me down and she's like, "They're gonna have to put you to sleep now." I remember her telling me, "You're just gonna go to sleep for like a couple of hours and then you're gonna wake up and you're gonna feel a lot better."

My mom had to leave the room while they were doing that. As she was walking out the door, the last thing I said was "Mom" and then I put my hands in a heart shape. That was the last thing I did and the last time my mom heard my voice for five weeks.

After I was intubated, things got worse. I had to be put on life support so needed to be moved to a bigger hospital in St. Louis, Missouri. The flight team came to evaluate me and they later told me they didn't think they were ever going to get me to Saint Louis. They thought I wasn't going to make the trip. But they said my mom was begging them to help me, everyone in my family was begging them, so they did everything they could to get me on the helicopter. They worked on me for several hours — every time they tried to move me something would go wrong — but eventually they got me there.
paras.zh: QUERY LENGTH LIMIT EXCEEDED. MAX ALLOWED QUERY : 500 CHARS

paras.en: The doctors had to call my parents to get permission to do surgery and put me on life support. My mom said that every time she heard my dad's phone ring, she thought they were calling to tell them that I didn't make it. They were told twice that it was more than likely I was going to pass than make it. They were trying to prepare my parents that I wasn't going to make it.

I woke up five weeks later, and it was very confusing. Everybody was told if I asked what day it was, just to tell me the day of the week. When someone accidentally told me the date, I started crying because my aunt was supposed to be getting married a few weeks later and I was worried about being at her wedding. My mom wasn't there, so my dad had to calm me down and then he told me the wedding had been pushed to October so I could be there.

The second thing I was worried about was that I was supposed to take a test on the Constitution and that I'd missed it. I ended up taking it in the hospital. I was there for 93 days. I got out the very last week of school, so I got to go in on the last day of school and surprise my classmates and my teachers.

That summer, I didn't really do anything besides go to doctor's appointments. I was doing physical therapy, occupational therapy and speech therapy — literally all my time was spent at the hospital in therapy. I'd missed three months of school, but I got to start eighth grade with all my friends, and I ended up playing basketball again. But the next several years was a lot of hard work of trying to get back to my normal.

It probably took the rest of junior high and high school to get back to how I would have been before. It was a very long process and during that time I got sick a lot, so I ended up back in the hospital several times. And it was hard going through that as a teenager — I felt like everybody else is living their normal life, and I felt like I missed out on a lot. Looking back now, I still feel like I did miss out a lot. But I think we made the best of the circumstances.

During COVID, when I was 22, I kept getting sick, and the doctors finally told me that part of my lung was so damaged from the flu it was causing infections, so they gave me an option of getting part of my lung removed. It was a major surgery, but I did it and that was probably the best decision I ever made, because it's been five years and I have not been in the hospital once.

I moved to Florida about three years ago, and I started working as a medical assistant in a pulmonary clinic. This semester I got accepted into respiratory therapy school, so for the next two years, I'm going to be in school for respiratory therapy. It's kind of a full circle moment, to come back into the medical field, because there was a point in my life where everybody was asking me, "Oh, do you want to be a doctor? Do you want to be a nurse?" And I'm like, "Absolutely not." I was still so sick that I was there all the time. I never wanted to be there.

- Trump's childhood vaccine order will threaten children's safety, even if it doesn't directly change policy
- Infectious diseases will seed new ground as the planet warms — here's where they'll spread

I went to college and I got a degree in criminal justice, but I never really knew what I wanted to do. I ended up getting a job at our local hospital — that first hospital that I went to. Every time they put me in the ER I just loved being there. That job made me realize that this is what I wanted to do.

When people hear my story, they don't realize that if I don't tell the end — after the hospital until now — they don't realize that my life didn't go back to normal after. It's taken 10 years. And it's hard. Some of the other family members that we've gotten to know through Families Fighting Flu, it's difficult listening to their stories. Sometimes I feel like I have this survivor's guilt. Their stories sound exactly like mine — but their kids didn't make it.

Before I got sick I got the flu shot every year, but that year we just got busy and it got put on the back burner. Since getting sick I have always made it a priority to get the flu shot every year. I know it is not a guarantee that I will never get the flu again — but hopefully it will reduce the chances of it ever getting that bad again.

articles.title: This Ancient 'Hell Chicken' Might Be the First Known Fruit-Loving Dinosaur, Revealing a Whole New Cretaceous Lifestyle

paras.en: When it comes to the Late Cretaceous period’s main characters, people tend to think of the terrifying, carnivorous Tyrannosaurus rex or the huge, long-necked, herbivorous sauropods. But the menu some 66 million to 100 million years ago offered more than just meat and veggies, and researchers have finally discovered evidence of a species taking advantage of it.

In a study published October 10 in the journal Nature Communications, researchers describe what might be the first known dinosaur that ate mostly fruit. The newly described Infernogallus jamesi had a mouth and jaw adapted to chewing soft foods similar to today’s frugivorous parrots. The findings shed new light on Cretaceous ecology and suggest that dinosaurs were more diverse than previously thought.

“It has been proposed before that some groups of dinosaurs ate fruits, but there was never evidence to back it up,” study co-author Thomas Dudgeon, an evolutionary ecologist at the Royal Ontario Museum in Canada, tells Reuters’ Will Dunham.

The genus name Infernogallus means “hell chicken.” That’s because of the creature’s small size and because the fossils, including a nearly complete skull and partial skeleton, were found in the Hell Creek Formation, a famous boneyard that stretches across Montana, the Dakotas and Wyoming. The species name jamesi honors the grandfather of one of the co-authors, who sparked the scientist’s love for paleontology.

I. jamesi weighed an estimated 25 pounds and was about the size of a turkey. It was one of the smallest caenagnathids—a group of beaked, two-legged, feathered dinosaurs—and lived in the same region and at the same time as the fearsome T. rex, around 67 million years ago. But the most notable aspect of the newly identified species was its chewing abilities.

“It’s pretty rare for animals to become specialized for a diet of fruit, so when it happens, it comes with some remarkable adaptations,” Dudgeon says in a statement. “The anatomy of Infernogallus is bizarre among dinosaurs, and we quickly realized that we were dealing with something special.”

Flowers are essential for pretty much all modern fruit-bearing plants. Their bright colors and scents serve as flashy billboards to attract pollinators. But before they evolved around 130 million years ago, plants used infrared heat to lure pollinating beetles, according to a study published in 2025.

The team created a digital reconstruction of the skull by CT scanning the fossils. Three key features pointed to a fruit-based diet: mouth muscles that enabled back-and-forth chewing, a special joint that allowed the jaw to slide forward, and ridges and grooves inside the beak that could help process soft materials like fruits. Today, this muscle organization exists in mammals with complex chewing abilities, including humans, as well as some fruit-eating birds like the vulturine parrot.

“This is a fantastic new dinosaur discovery,” Steve Brusatte, a paleontologist at the University of Edinburgh in Scotland who did not participate in the study, tells Science’s Taylor Mitchell Brown. “This new species finally reveals the face of a dinosaur fruit eater,” he adds. “We can now be sure that at least some dinosaurs were enjoying Cretaceous fruit salads.”

I. jamesi’s fruit salad probably included drupes, which had soft flesh around a hard seed or pit, similar to today’s cherries and peaches, Greg Funston, lead author of the study and a paleontologist at Stony Brook University, tells the outlet. In fact, when Funston and colleagues investigated the evolution of the hell chicken and drupes, they discovered that the dinosaur’s lineage started to adapt to its specialized diet right as these fruits became larger and more abundant. The finding represents a rare clear connection between dinosaur diversity and the evolution of flowering plants.

paras.en: Furthermore, fruit-eating dinosaurs may have helped these plants spread by dispersing their seeds through their feces. The fossil record shows that during the Cretaceous, flowering plants became the most prominent land-based vegetation.

“We know that these big-seeded fruits were proliferating and spreading, and it seems like caenagnathids could have fit this role—although we feel more evidence is needed before drawing that link confidently,” Funston tells Reuters.

articles.title: Was the British King Who Urged the Romans to Invade Actually a Queen? One Archaeologist Thinks So

paras.en: In 43 C.E., the Roman Emperor Claudius invaded Britain, leading to its transformation it into an imperial province for nearly 400 years. This invasion was launched at the behest of an ousted British king named Verica, who fled across the English Channel to seek Roman aid. Now, a British archaeologist suggests that Verica was no king at all, but rather a queen.

The reassessment by Miles Russell, an archaeologist at Bournemouth University, reinterprets one of the most consequential figures of the late British Iron Age. Writing in Current Archaeology, Russell argues that “the assumption that this powerful ruler must have been male reflects a degree of unconscious bias, and perhaps a hangover from the patriarchal mindset of early Classicists.”

Verica was a Roman ally who led the Atrebates, a tribe whose territory spanned modern-day Berkshire, Hampshire and West Sussex. Around 40 C.E., during territorial upheavals following the death of powerful tribal leader Cunobelinus and the ascent of his son Caratacus, Verica was deposed and fled to Rome.

Roman historian Cassius Dio, writing in the early third century C.E., recorded that a Briton called “Berikos,” or “Bericus,” appealed directly to Claudius, handing the emperor a pretext for invasion. Without this appeal, “it’s likely that Rome would never have invaded,” Russell tells Gizmodo’s Ed Cara.
He adds: “Verica was a major player in the story of how Britain became a Roman province and has been discussed in many books, papers and articles, but has always been misgendered.”

Numismatic evidence also presents a striking departure from standard Iron Age coinage. While contemporary male leaders like Cunobelinus decorated their currency with overtly masculine warriors, coins struck under Verica depict “slender, bare-breasted equestrian figures that appear irrefutably female,” Russell writes.

Furthermore, some of Verica’s coins have the Latin abbreviation “COM F,” which is traditionally translated as Commios filius, or the “son of Commios,” a leader of the Atrebates tribe who allied with Julius Caesar during his invasion of Gaul. As Russell points out, that could just as easily denote Commios filia, or “daughter of Commios.” While the coins carry the Latin title “rex,” Russell argues that the designation is a “non-gender specific title” that shows Verica ruled with the “the full authorization of the emperor,” according to a statement.
paras.zh: QUERY LENGTH LIMIT EXCEEDED. MAX ALLOWED QUERY : 500 CHARS

paras.en: A female Verica could also explain the sharp anti-Claudius barbs in classical accounts by Roman chroniclers, who frequently portrayed the emperor as an easily swayed, “henpecked” figure, Russell writes.

Presenting Claudius’ invasion as prompted by a woman fits this narrative pattern. “In effect, [Cassius] Dio was saying that the campaign was undertaken solely because of the whisperings of a barbarian femme fatale,” Russell explains in the statement.

The idea also fits recent insights into the period. In 2025, Russell co-authored a study of ancient southern British cemeteries showing that Iron Age communities were matrilocal: Women remained settled in their ancestral communities while men moved, suggesting land and status were passed down the female line.

Under Roman rule, Britain was a highly urbanized place with tiled-roofs, road networks and a coinage system. Centuries after the Romans left, however, Britons had gone back to living in homes with thatched roofs and reverted from market-based trades to subsistence farming.

However, not all scholars are convinced. Katharina Rebay-Salisbury, an archaeologist at the University of Vienna, remains skeptical of the numismatic evidence. “I find it a bit difficult to differentiate a naked female body from a naked male body in these very stylized images,” she tells New Scientist.

Roger Tomlin, a specialist in Roman epigraphy at University of Oxford, tells the Guardian’s Nicola Davis that while the feminine “-a” ending is plausible, Cassius Dio explicitly assumed the ruler was male, referring to him as “Bericus.” He also disputes Russell’s claim that “rex” had been used for both male and female rulers.

Russell welcomes the scholarly debate. “If it does create debate and argument, I think that's for the better,” he tells the Guardian. “The one-sided story’s been there for so long. We need that to change.”

articles.title: A Nazi Submarine Torpedoed a Merchant Ship Just Off the Coast of Maine in 1944. Divers Have Finally Located the Wreckage, 400 Feet Below the Surface

paras.en: In December 1944, a Nazi submarine torpedoed a Canadian merchant ship off the coast of Maine, killing 43 crew members on board. Now, more than eight decades later, divers say they’ve located the long-lost World War II wreck.

The SS Cornwallis was discovered submerged nearly 400 feet deep in the northwest Atlantic Ocean near Mount Desert Rock, about 25 miles from the Maine mainland. Members of the Nomad Exploration Team, a self-funded civilian technical dive team based in Portsmouth, New Hampshire, found the nearly 5,500-ton vessel after years of searching.

The Cornwallis was traveling from Barbados to New Brunswick to deliver sugar and molasses when its forward cargo hold was struck by a torpedo from a German U-boat on December 3, 1944. Only five of the 48 crew members survived. They found life rafts, which were eventually spotted by aircraft. The survivors were picked up by fishing boats and transferred to a U.S. Navy rescue vessel, which delivered them to Rockland, Maine.

Days earlier, the submarine had dropped off two Nazi spies near Hancock, Maine, as part of “Operation Magpie.” The spies—William C. Colepaugh, a 26-year-old American Nazi sympathizer, and Erich Gimpel, a 35-year-old German native—caught a taxi to Bangor, then took a train to Portland. They eventually reached New York City, where they stayed for several weeks before Colepaugh turned himself in to the FBI. Both men were originally sentenced to death, but President Harry Truman commuted their sentences down to 30 years.
paras.zh: QUERY LENGTH LIMIT EXCEEDED. MAX ALLOWED QUERY : 500 CHARS

paras.en: Meanwhile, the Cornwallis’ location remained unknown. The Nomad Exploration Team started looking for the Cornwallis in 2019, using historical records to narrow down the search to three potential locations. They made five total trips to search for the wreck, ultimately investigating more than 50 square miles of seafloor with side-scan sonar.

They found a wreck that seemed likely to be the Cornwallis on July 11, which was a moment of “exhilaration,” Danny Allan, a founding member of the group, tells the Portsmouth Herald’s Ian Lenahan. When they dove down to confirm its identity, however, they repeatedly encountered challenging conditions.

“It’s very deep, it’s very cold, a lot of current,” Jeff Goodreau, a member of the dive team, tells the Portland Press Herald’s Drew Johnson. “Pretty much the worst-case scenario as far as diving goes.”
In the end, they used the Cornwallis’ blueprints to confirm the wreck as the missing ship, the Bangor Daily News’ Sabrina Martin reports.

The Cornwallis isn’t the first shipwreck the Nomad Exploration Team has successfully located. In 2017, they found the SS William H. Machen, a cargo ship that sank in 1942 off the coast of Portsmouth. A year later, they located the USS Eagle 56, a warship sunk by a German torpedo in April 1945 off Cape Elizabeth, Maine.

They decided to go after the Cornwallis because it was the largest missing vessel in all of New England. They were also intrigued by the ship’s history. Two years before it sank off the coast of Maine, the ship was torpedoed by a German U-boat while sailing in Barbados. It partially sank, but was refloated, repaired and returned to service. It’s one of just five ships known to have been torpedoed and sunk twice, per the Halifax Chronicle Herald’s Ian Fairclough.

According to the divers, the wreck is located in federal waters. The state of Maine can’t claim ownership of it, nor can the U.S. Navy, meaning it “belongs to everyone and no one,” Allan explains to the Bangor Daily News.

“We could file paperwork to take ownership of it, [but] we’re not planning to do that,” he adds. “For us, the real reward is to find the wreck, put a place on the map [and] give closure to the families.”

The team also hopes the discovery shines a light on how close the war came to the shores of New England. Though it wasn’t a military vessel, the Cornwallis was equipped with machine guns and had seven armed guards on board when it sank.

Looking ahead, the divers plan to return to the wreck site and continue exploring it using a remotely operated underwater vehicle. They’ve also identified their next target, Allan tells the Portsmouth Herald. He wouldn’t share the name of the vessel, revealing only that it's a “very large wreck, several hundred feet long [that] went down with all hands on deck.”

articles.title: GoRuck Black Friday Sale: My Favorite Packs and Weighted Vests Are Nearly 50% Off
articles.author: Scott Gilbertson

paras.en: GoRuck has launched its Black Friday Sale with plenty of great deals for anyone who, like me, wants to work out without the need for a gym. I've never liked going to the gym. I work from home, and I work out at home, mostly bodyweight exercises and calisthenics, with some extra weight in the form of GoRuck sandbags and kettlebells.

This book of bodyweight exercises has been my workout bible for years, but I also love hiking, or as the cool kids call it, rucking. Rucking is hiking, with some extra weight on your back. You don't need any special gear to ruck; just a backpack and some sand will get you going. But put 20 pounds in your average day pack, and you'll quickly discover it's not very well made. When you wear through what you've got, get a GoRuck. They're nigh on indestructible, have a lifetime warranty, and they're purpose-built for rucking (but make a great daypack as well).

paras.en: Luckily, GoRuck has launched its Black Friday sale, with the company's Basic Rucker pack available for nearly half off, just $79 ($76 off).

This is a phenomenal deal on a pack that's going to last you a lifetime. The smaller volume of the Basic Rucker keeps the weight high and tight on your back, which makes it more stable and less prone to shifting when you're off balance.

Grab yourself a weight plate too. They aren't on sale, and you can, as noted above, get by with sandbags or anything else heavy, but the ruck plates are nice to have. I suggest starting at 10 pounds if you're brand new to rucking, 20 pounds if you're in reasonable shape, and 30 pounds if you already work out regularly and are just looking to try something new.

I should note that I also have a USA-made GoRuck GR1, and it is a far, far nicer pack overall than the Basic Rucker, but I like the GR1 less for rucking. The Basic Rucker is actually what I ruck/hike in on a daily basis, and it's really all you need. (I reserve the GR1 for day hikes and travel.)

If you do feel like splashing out, though, there's an even better deal going right now at GoRuck: Spend $300, and you get a 14L Basic Rucker free. So you can grab yourself a USA-made GoRuck GR1 for $395 (sorry, not on sale) and get the Basic Rucker free.

If rucking doesn't grab you, but the idea of skipping the gym does, my new favorite GoRuck gear is the Achilles Weighted Vest, which is on sale for $139 ($86 off). I've been using this for about six months now, and it has added a whole new level to my bodyweight workouts. It's not what I'd want for running (the Rucking Weight Vest seems the better option for that), but for making pull-ups, dips, and push-ups 20 pounds harder, the Achilles is fantastic. The Spy Ruck above is the women's version of the weighted vest (my wife loves hers).

articles.title: This Totally Free App Can Free Up Space on Your Mac
articles.author: Justin Pot

paras.en: Your Mac's hard drive is full ... again. What's taking up all that space? Endless applications promise to answer this question and help you free up space, most with a subscription. I've tested many over the years, and few are easier to recommend than Purge.
paras.zh: Mac的硬盘又满了。是什么占据了这么多空间？无穷无尽的应用程序有望回答这个问题，并帮助您释放空间，大多数应用程序都是通过订阅来实现的。这些年来，我已经测试了很多次，很少有比Purge更容易推荐的。

paras.en: This totally free, open source app gives you a quick breakdown of what's taking up space on your hard drive and offers a few specific ways to free it up. Even better: There are no ads or upsells. Purge can even delete Apple Intelligence's offline models from macOS 27, which could free up over 10 GB.
paras.zh: 这个完全免费的开源应用程序为您提供了硬盘空间占用情况的快速细分，并提供了一些释放空间的具体方法。更好的是：没有广告或追加销售。Purge甚至可以从macOS 27中删除Apple Intelligence的离线型号，这可以释放超过10 GB的空间。

paras.en: But even if you want to keep Apple's AI features, you can still clear up plenty of space. Your Mac, like any computer, tends to build up clutter over time. Sure, you might have forgotten about the games, images, and videos you downloaded, but caches also take up space. These are files downloaded and saved to speed things up, which can be useful. The problem is they can stick around longer than necessary and take up space. And then there are caches and settings left behind by apps you uninstalled ages ago—they're still there, eating up precious bytes.
paras.zh: QUERY LENGTH LIMIT EXCEEDED. MAX ALLOWED QUERY : 500 CHARS

paras.en: Purge is designed to help you clean all that out, but it can do more. It's built around lists of files known to be safe to purge. There's also a list of things it will never touch, including crucial system files and your own documents. Finally, Purge sends files to the Trash instead of deleting them outright, so you can always recover them if something breaks.
To get started, download Purge and install it. Open the application, and it will show you what's taking up space on your Mac.

If you want, click the Clean Safe Items button, and the app will handle it, assuming you trust it. I recommend paying a bit more attention, though. First, delete some caches. You'll see a list of caches, all of which are safe to purge periodically.
You'll also see Apple's Aerial screen savers here. These videos are very cool, but take up a lot of space—delete them if you, like most 21st-century people, don't use a screen saver.
There's also a Dev Tools section, which isn't relevant for most people. If you use Homebrew, though, don't skip this—it's an easy way to delete cached installation files you don't need anymore.
The next tool shows you only the largest files on your computer, likely videos or other large media. I ended up moving a few things I'd forgotten about off my laptop—I bet you'll find something, too.

Up next is a tool for uninstalling apps. Note that this doesn't just remove the application—it also removes every file associated with it, including your settings, caches, and anything the application downloaded. Deleting applications in Finder doesn't do this, meaning you might leave all kinds of files behind.

Speaking of that, there's also a tool that shows leftover data from applications you've already deleted. In my case, it was several gigabytes, all basically wasted. I highly recommend checking this section and deleting anything large that you're confident you won't use again.

Finally, so long as we're talking about things you're not using, there's Apple Intelligence. Apple's most recent operating systems come preloaded with offline AI models, which power things like notification summaries, writing suggestions, and the new AI-powered Siri. You might like and use these features, but if not, Apple removed the toggle in macOS 27 that lets you disable them altogether.

That's why Purge has one final tool that can completely remove the Apple Intelligence models. Click it, and you'll see a list of installed models above a delete button. Click the button, and Purge will delete the models and prevent macOS from reinstalling them.
These features are why I plan on keeping Purge around. It's a great way to see what's taking up space on your drive and then do something about it.

articles.title: The Best Cat Water Fountains of 2026: Petlibro, Petkit, Oneisall
articles.author: Molly Higgins

paras.en: As seen with the rise of automatic litter boxes, automatic feeders, pet trackers, and now cat water fountains, technology has made it so that we can take care of our pets without having to do as much of the manual labor.
paras.zh: 随着自动宠物砂盒、自动喂食器、宠物追踪器以及现在的猫咪饮水机的兴起，技术已经使我们能够照顾我们的宠物，而无需做太多的体力劳动。

paras.en: These fancy fountains don't just make our lives easier. They can also help cats stay hydrated and live healthier. Ever wonder why your cat can't resist a dripping faucet but ignores its water bowl? In the wild, cats are drawn to moving water, since stagnant puddles can harbor bacteria. A water fountain plays into this natural instinct, encouraging cats to drink more. These techy fountains are also often connected to an app, which sends reminders and tracks drinking habits.
paras.zh: 这些花哨的喷泉不仅让我们的生活更轻松。它们还可以帮助猫咪保持水分，活得更健康。有没有想过为什么你的猫不能忍受一个滴水的水龙头，却忽略了它的水碗？在野外，猫被流动的水吸引，因为停滞的水坑可能藏有细菌。喷泉发挥了这种自然本能，鼓励猫咪多喝水。这些高科技的喷泉也经常连接到应用程序，该应用程序会发送提醒并跟踪饮酒习惯。

paras.en: After prolonged testing, I now look for these three things when shopping for an automatic cat water fountain: a wireless pump for easier cleaning, stainless steel (or glass) construction so it's more hygienic, and a window to monitor water levels (especially if it's not connected to an app). I think the Petkit EverSweet Ultra with AI Camera Pet Water Fountain is the overall best cat water fountain, and the cheaper Oneisall 3.5L Cord-Free Pet Water Fountain is the best choice for most people who are on a budget.

paras.en: Cheerble Pet Fountain Elfin E1+ for $70: I don't love the plastic components of this fountain, but otherwise I have no complaints. It has intermittent flow that goes off when it senses a cat is near, and the top lights indicate things like filter replacement and battery level. Overall, it was super easy to clean this model because everything sits on one another, and it has few parts and a wireless pump. It didn't stand out enough to make the top picks, but I do recommend it if you're OK with cleaning more frequently because of the plastic design.

paras.en: Petlibro Capsule Dog Fountain for $45: Petlibro’s Capsule Dog Fountain is right at snout level for my small dogs, which I prefer for when they eat and drink to prevent choking. Despite not being as high-tech (there's no app connectivity like some of our other tested options), it’s become a reliable tool for us. I can see this working well for parents of rambunctious dogs who don’t need high-tech functionality, just something consistent. —Julia Forbes

But this is a solid, whisper-quiet stainless steel fountain that has worked reliably. I love the adjustable spout, and my pets seem to prefer it over some other models I've tried.

paras.en: Petkit Eversweet 3 Pro for $63: Like many other styles we tested, this circular automatic fountain connects to power via USB and has an app to monitor water levels and remind you when it’s time to fill or change the filter. The top part also has a small reservoir that leaves a couple of ounces accessible during a power outage. Although the top is made of plastic, there's a filter with three layers (replacements are $20), a pump with a foam filter, and a UV light to further sterilize water by killing potentially harmful bacteria. Like many of Petkit's products, the app is lacking. When I went out of town, the app had trouble adjusting to the time change and didn’t send me a notification that water levels were low. When I got back home, the machine had stopped the water flow without alerting me via the app.
paras.zh: QUERY LENGTH LIMIT EXCEEDED. MAX ALLOWED QUERY : 500 CHARS

paras.en: Petlibro Capsule Fountain for $37: A solid, inexpensive choice, this fountain is made from BPA-free plastic and has a five-layer filtration system and stainless steel top reservoir. There's a transparent water tank for easier monitoring, and it comes in a bunch of cute colors. The spout is tall and has a continuous flow, making it ideal for cats who love to drink from faucets. However, it's not connected to an app, so you'll have to monitor water levels and set manual reminders for filter replacement and cleaning. The plastic is also harder to clean, and it has a wired pump, which makes cleaning trickier. It works effectively, but there are better options out there at this price point.
paras.zh: QUERY LENGTH LIMIT EXCEEDED. MAX ALLOWED QUERY : 500 CHARS

paras.en: Petkit Eversweet Max for $76: This techy automatic fountain is battery-powered (lasting up to 83 days on a charge), and the drinking bowl is made of stainless steel, but the reservoir is plastic. Because of the shape of the basin with the chunky battery and reservoir bowl, it’s a little awkward to clean. The app logs every time a pet drinks and compares it over time to determine whether your cat’s drinking habits have changed. The app also keeps track of when the filter needs replacing and when you last added water. However, it doesn’t monitor or show how much water is left in the basin; you have to check manually. The design also made it a bit difficult to clean and refill easily.
paras.zh: QUERY LENGTH LIMIT EXCEEDED. MAX ALLOWED QUERY : 500 CHARS

paras.en: Enabot Rola Smart Pet Water Fountain for $30: Cordless and running on a rechargeable battery that lasts up to 60 days (although it can stay plugged in, too), this fountain has a wireless pump that uses magnetic induction—one of the easiest and most hassle-free pumps to clean of all I tested. The fountain has a stainless steel top that holds a decent amount of water even when not running. However, the tank is plastic—I’m wary of plastic because of its propensity to harbor bacteria (plus it doesn't keep water as cold). The app gives reminders of when the water’s low, the fountain needs cleaning, or the filter needs replacing, plus it automatically stops dispensing water and sends you a reminder to refill via its app. It also logs the number of times your pet drank and for how long, monitoring hydration patterns over time. A complaint I had is that this fountain wouldn’t stay on continuous stream mode, even when plugged in, instead automatically switching to the motion-sensing stream.

paras.en: Homerunpet Wireless Pet Fountain for $60: This cordless fountain can be used as a traditional fountain plugged in on its base, or can be detached and moved around the house with 30 days of battery life. I don't love that this fountain is all plastic, but it's easy to see water levels from the outside, the top and filter layers are super easy to remove, clean, and replace, and the wireless (basically silent) pump makes it a whole lot easier to clean. Plastic doesn't keep the water as cold or clean as stainless steel, so you'll have to clean it a lot more often. The fountain only begins bubbling when a cat (or human) approaches to save battery power, and there's no option to control the flow (and no connected app). I like the wireless pump, but I'm really over plastic at this point.

paras.en: Wonder Creature Cat Fountain for $18: My two cats have cycled through several water fountains over the past few years, but this no-nonsense version has been a stalwart. The inside is lit by a blue LED (bright enough to glow in the dark), and a clear viewing window on the side makes it easy to monitor the water level from afar. I also like the dishwasher-safe metal bowl and the fact that you can remove parts of the white-and-yellow flower to create a fountain configuration your cat likes (waterfall, low bubble-up, tall bubble-up). The only major downsides are the fact that it requires very frequent cleaning and filter changes due to the plastic body, and that there is no reservoir to hold water in case of a power outage or pump malfunction. When I went on vacation, I had to swap it out for an old-school gravity dispenser. —Kat Merck

paras.en: Happy & Polly Gothic Cat Drinking Fountain for $66: If you prefer gothic decor to neutral blandness, this ghostly ceramic cat fountain from Happy & Polly may tempt you to bite. The water bubbles up out of the top of the ghost and pools on the ceramic top. It’s fairly quiet at around 35 decibels, but it gets loud when the water is running low, and I worry about the motor burning out, as the 1.5-liter capacity can run dry fast. While the ceramic finish is easy to clean, it is fiddly to take apart. You will want to clean it once a week to prevent it from becoming slimy, and you must change the filter once a month. —Simon Hill

paras.en: Petkit Eversweet Solo 2 for $45: I love three key features of this fountain: The bowl sits on top of a wireless charging base, so you don’t have to fiddle with cables; it is super easy to clean, and it's very quiet at around 25 decibels. A flashing light warns you when the water is running low, and you can check when the filter needs to be changed in the app. There’s an optional smart mode that pumps intermittently and a night mode to turn the light off. Pleasingly, all three of our cats drink from this fountain, though that does mean I have to refill it often, as it only holds 2 liters. —Simon Hill

paras.en: Oneisall Stainless Steel Pet Fountain for $43: This drinking fountain is about as simple as they come. As it's designed for cats or small dogs, it has a large bowl, but some cats will prefer that. I love the mostly stainless steel construction, as it's easy to keep clean and less prone to dirt and bacteria buildup. You can even stick parts into the dishwasher. This fountain can hold up to 7 liters of water, so you don’t have to refill as often. It’s fairly quiet at around 35 decibels, but it gets louder when the water is running low (a red light warns you when it needs a refill). You should clean once a week and rinse the filter. The filter packs are relatively affordable, and you need to swap them once a month. —Simon Hill

paras.en: PetSnowy OilClear AI Series Wireless Weight-Sensing Pet Fountain for $90: I was initially intrigued and confused by this fountain, but by the end of testing, I actually ended up throwing it away. (Mother Gaia weeps.) One big sell is the built-in gravity-sensing technology that tracks your pet’s daily water intake while accounting for natural evaporation. The other is a head-scratcher: There's real-time thermostatic heating to keep water warm year-round. Huh?? Do pets like warm water? Is this a thing I'm not aware of? It's rechargeable and can be operated cord-free with the battery, and it has a connected app to monitor usage. It has sensor-activated smart water dispensing, which dispenses water when cats approach. As time went on, the flow got weaker and weaker, and after about two weeks of testing, the water stopped flowing altogether. I was not able to fix it.

paras.en: Petcube Ceramic Pet Water Fountain for $90: I really wanted to love this fountain; although its basin is plastic, it has a ceramic top, which is more hygienic than plastic (plus, I had never tested a ceramic model before), and the brand makes some of my favorite pet cameras. However, setup was a bit confusing; it took a long time to get the base charged to power the fountain's water flow, and the sensor to start the water flow can only be triggered from one side, making placement awkward. After a few days, it would only run while plugged in. Soon, its stream was barely strong enough to reach the top, and after just over a week, it stopped working altogether. Also, it's overly expensive for what it is.

paras.en: Cat Mate 3-Level Pet Fountain for $28: This tall automatic Cat Mate fountain sets itself apart with three tiers for cats who like to drink at every level. Cleaning the motor requires disassembly using tools and extended soaking. Because of the long distance the water has to travel, it evaporates quickly and needs to be refilled about every other day. Plastic also harbors bacteria, and previous plastic models I’ve owned have had mold issues. The basin is quite large and sits flat. Because of this, some debris lingers in the front rather than flowing to the filter system behind. The plastic material and fact the basin doesn’t direct debris toward the filter caused this fountain to become dirtier faster than others.

paras.en: Whisker City Free Fall Cat Fountain for $30: This huge fountain is better suited for dogs, with its 150-fluid-ounce bowl and waterfall design. Although the basin has a small splash pad to help offset the waterfall noise, this was one of the loudest fountains I tested. The evaporation from the waterfall-like system also caused me to refill it every other day. Because of the structure of the fountain, my cats had to bend their head at an awkward angle. They tended to avoid drinking from the basin because of that, and their heads got slightly wet from the splatter of the waterfall. The basin is also not angled, so crumbs and debris sit at the bottom of the bowl.

paras.en: Petkit EverSweet Solo SE for $26: This very simple, straightforward fountain has a square-shaped body, is translucent to easily see water levels from the outside, and has a nearly silent 25-decibel wireless pump to circulate water from the basin to the top level, where 2 ounces of water are always available for drinking, even in case of power failure. The basin sits on a base and all parts easily detach, making it easier to clean. This fountain doesn’t have multiple modes or an associated app—you’ll have to check water levels manually. I noticed this fountain didn't keep water as cold as some of the others, and because of the design of the top, debris often pooled in the dipped areas, which required more frequent cleaning.

paras.en: I used each fountain for at least a week as my cats’ main water source. As mentioned, I noted the ease of setup, evaluated parts and filters, and generally compared the various types of water fountains—spigot, bubbling, or waterfall. Some flows were continuous, and some were intermittent (my cats didn’t prefer intermittent). Cats may also be intrigued and want to play with the machine rather than drink, so be sure to give them time and keep another water source around until they are fully adjusted to the new gadget.
paras.zh: QUERY LENGTH LIMIT EXCEEDED. MAX ALLOWED QUERY : 500 CHARS

paras.en: Cats sometimes struggle to consume enough water, which can lead to potentially lethal UTIs and blockages, especially in male cats. This is one of the reasons vets are moving toward encouraging owners to give their cat at least a partially wet-food diet, as this helps them consume more moisture, especially since cats don’t naturally drink as much as dogs. Also, unlike dogs, cats are generally quite particular in their likes and dislikes, and cats can see stagnant water as potentially harmful. (If the cat were in the wild, stagnant water has more potential for harmful bacteria). Cats are more drawn to moving water in nature, and these fountains help encourage them to drink more by emulating what they’re naturally drawn to.
paras.zh: QUERY LENGTH LIMIT EXCEEDED. MAX ALLOWED QUERY : 500 CHARS

paras.en: While automatic water fountains are better for cats' overall water consumption, they do require a bit more work and money. Rather than refilling a bowl, these take a little elbow grease—but it’s worth it for your cat’s health. Along with routine refilling and cleaning, you’ll need to disassemble the fountain to clean all parts, including using a brush for the bowl and tubes. You may also have to disassemble the motor to deep-clean mineral buildup. There are different types of filtration cartridges in specific shapes for the brand’s fountains, which require you to buy and change out filters, usually monthly but sometimes more often.
paras.zh: QUERY LENGTH LIMIT EXCEEDED. MAX ALLOWED QUERY : 500 CHARS

paras.en: Let’s be honest, a lot of these fountains are pretty much the same. I looked especially for the overall design—I am a fiend for stainless steel because of the potential of porous plastic harboring harmful bacteria. I also favor a wide reservoir without high sides to help reduce the chance of whisker fatigue. I prefer fountains that have a small basin reservoir of water available at all times, in case of low water levels or power failure. I took into account ease of setting up, refilling, and cleaning, as well as overall design. And of course, there were some that my cats took to straight away, and some they didn’t seem to favor as much.
paras.zh: QUERY LENGTH LIMIT EXCEEDED. MAX ALLOWED QUERY : 500 CHARS

paras.en: After prolonged testing, I now look for these three things and encourage you to as well: a cordless pump for easier (and safer) cleaning, hygienic stainless-steel construction, and a window to monitor water levels (especially if it's not connected to an app).
paras.zh: 经过长时间的测试，我现在寻找这三件事，并鼓励您也这样做：无绳泵，以便更轻松（更安全）地清洁，卫生的不锈钢结构，以及监控水位的窗口（特别是如果它没有连接到应用程序）。
